editorial.headline: Kitchen & Tableware Retail: Open Nationally, Closed to PMA in Bali
editorial.standfirst: This retail activity welcomes fully foreign ownership nationally, while Bali’s permanent PMA moratorium closes the registration route on the island.
editorial.body:
In Bali, a foreign investor cannot register this activity today. That is the practical starting point for a retail business dealing in crockery, kitchen supplies and tableware: national investment policy calls it TERBUKA and allows full foreign ownership, but Bali’s PMA position is blocked. The distinction matters because the national permission is real, yet it does not create a Bali registration route. The record’s Bali status, Blocked (risk class), identifies a restriction tied to risk class rather than a softened local qualification.

The commercial subject is richly specific. It is retail trade in fragile household tableware and the tools surrounding cooking, serving and storing food: plates, basins, bowls, cups, teapots, spoons, forks and food carriers; jars and baby bottles; pots, trays, buckets, thermoses and jerry cans; as well as mortars and pestles, coconut graters, cutting boards, ladles, baskets, steaming vessels, food covers, satay skewers and meat grinders. Taken together, the scope describes the everyday material culture of the kitchen and dining table, from the vessel that holds a meal to the implement that prepares it.

Nationally, this activity is open to PMA. The maximum foreign share recorded is 100%, so the national position permits a business in this activity to be fully foreign-owned. The record also opens it across the Mikro, Kecil, Menengah and Besar scales. At each of those stated scales, the activity remains the retail provision of this defined range of household goods. The scale labels establish the stated range of business scale; the slim record gives no further ranking or condition within them.

Bali changes the result without changing what the activity is. For the Besar scale, the record states that every scope is OSS Low or Medium-Low risk. Bali’s permanent, island-wide moratorium blocks PMA for activities carrying either of those risk levels, and the record dates this block to May 13, 2026. It is therefore not accurate to present the 100% national ceiling as a Bali opportunity: for a foreign investor seeking to register this activity in Bali, the answer is no today. The relevant local constraint is the moratorium documented under Gubernur letter B.27.000/642/PM/DPMPTSP.
editorial.pullQuote: National permission is real, yet it does not create a Bali registration route.
